newsitem.title: USA: IMF says global expansion should continue.
newsitem.headline: IMF says global expansion should continue.

text.p: Alver Carlson
The global economy should enjoy its fastest growth in nearly a decade this year and shows little indication of heading for trouble, the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday.
"There are few signs of the tensions and imbalances that usually foreshadow significant downturns in the business cycle," the report said.

Global inflation remains subdued, policymakers seem steadfastly committed to price stability, countries are trying to live within their means, the interest rate outlook seems favorable and currencies are generally in line, the report added.

But the IMF, in its semi-annual World Economic Outlook, did raise red flags about the impact of embedded unemployment in Europe and the possibility of an even more severe stock market retreat than has occured in recent weeks.

"Recent declines in equity prices have underscored the risk of a more significant correction, especially if earnings expectations were to be downgraded or a reemergence of inflationay pressures were to require a marked increase in interest rates," the IMF said.
It estimated that the global economy would grow 4.4 percent this year and next, the fastest pace since a 4.7 percent rise in 1988. The world economy grew 4.0 percent last year.
It estimated that the major industrial countries overall would grow by 2.6 percent this year and next compared with 2.2 percent in 1996.

The United States, it said, would grow by 3.0 percent this year after growing 2.4 percent in 1996 and then turn lower next year to 2.2 percent. Germany is forecast to grow 2.3 percent this year and 3.0 percent in 1998 after rising a tepid 1.4 percent in 1996.
Japan, however, is forecast to slow to 2.2 percent this year and 2.9 percent in 1998 after growing 3.6 percent in 1996.

Developing countries, for their part, are seen as growing 6.6 percent this year and 6.5 percent in 1998, identical with 1996. Economies in transition such as the former Soviet Union are seen as growing 3.0 percent this year and 4.8 percent in 1998. They edged up by only 0.1 percent in 1996.

The report noted that the Federal Reserve attempted to slightly cool the expanding U.S. economy by raising interest rates last month and may need to do so again to keep inflationary pressures from breaking out.

"Given the strong underlying growth momentum, a moderate firming of monetary conditions may soon be needed and is assumed in the forecast," the IMF said. Fed policymakers meet again May 20 to discuss rates.

While the report seemed generally satisfied with the foreign exchange levels, saying they were consistent with underlying economic fundamentals, it did raise questions about the impact of the rise of the dollar are against the yen.
"These currency movements may be reversed as cyclical positions become less uneven," the IMF said.

The IMF said that easy monetary policy and improved labor market conditions in Japan should underpin a moderate pace of recovery this year and that the Japanese authorities should keep policy relaxed until the recovery is firmly established.
Moreover, the IMF cautioned Japan that it must tighten its budget at a sustained pace so that it doesn't undermine the prospects for continued recovery.

"Although there is potential for growth to turn out stronger than expected, uncertainties remain about the impact of fiscal consolidation measures and the effects of strains in the financial system," the report said.

Short-term interest rates have beem reduced considerably in both Germany and France to help offset recessionary sources, but it is still too early to conclude that rate cutting has run its course, the report said.

Britain, in the midst of a solid upswing that is in its fifth year, must keep an eye on inflation and should tighten monetary policy early to reduce the risk, the report said. The pound's rise was helping dampen inflation pressures and posed no immediate threat to the expansion, said the IMF.

Turning to the economic targets designed to underpin the formation of the European Monetary Union, the report said that Germany, France and Italy may need to do more to meet the requirement that budget deficits be no more than 3.0 percent of gross domestic product.
